title: Max formula for cyclic covering dimensions of invariant direct sums
statement:
Let $q$ be a prime power, let $sigma$ be an operator with $sigma^n=\operatorname{id}$, and let $W_1$ and $W_2$ be $sigma$-invariant subspaces satisfying

$$
\mathbb{F}_{q^n}=W_1\oplus W_2.
$$

Write $h_{\sigma}(V)$ for the corresponding cyclic covering parameter of a $sigma$-invariant subspace $V$. **The max-formula conjecture.** One has

$$
h_q(n)=h_{\sigma}(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})=\max\{h_{\sigma}(W_1),h_{\sigma}(W_2)\}.
$$

The preceding discussion establishes the inequality with the maximum as a lower bound; the conjecture asserts equality for every such invariant direct-sum decomposition. No resolution is given in the source.
references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04558

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of February 2026).
source_name: Yangcheng Li, Pingzhi Yuan, Shuang Li and Yuanpeng Zeng, “On cyclically covering subspaces of F^n_q”, arXiv:2602.04558 (2026).

progress.label: Open · solution reported
progress.tldr: A reader-written construction claims a counterexample in dimension $15$, but no independent verification has appeared.
progress.summary:
Li, Yuan, Li, and Zeng posed the max-formula conjecture in a February 2026 preprint. It asks whether the cyclic covering parameter of every invariant direct sum equals the larger parameter of its two summands.

*[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04558)*

**Known results**

- The general lower bound $h_{\sigma}(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})\ge\max\{h_{\sigma}(W_1),h_{\sigma}(W_2)\}$ is proved.
- Equality holds if one summand has parameter $0$.
- Equality holds when $h_q(n)=1$.
- Equality holds for the known values $h_q(q^d-1)=d-1$.


**Posted attempt**

A reader-written construction claims a complete counterexample with $q=2$, $n=15$, and invariant summands having parameters $1$ and $2$, while the whole space has parameter $3$. Thus it claims $h_{\sigma}(\mathbb{F}_{2^{15}})>\max\{h_{\sigma}(W_1),h_{\sigma}(W_2)\}$. The attempt has not been independently verified.

Current status (as of August 2026): The lower bound and listed special cases are settled, while the universal max-formula conjecture is disputed by an unverified claimed counterexample.

*Caveats. The counterexample is reader-written and has no corroborating publication or independent verification in the retrieved sources.*

solutions.body:
The conjecture is false, even when its first equality holds. Take \(q=2\) and \(n=15\), and identify the \(\mathbb F_2\)-vector space \(\mathbb F_{2^{15}}\) with
\[
V=\mathbb F_4\oplus\mathbb F_2^9\oplus\mathbb F_{16}.
\]
Choose \(\alpha\in\mathbb F_4^\times\) of order \(3\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb F_{16}^\times\) of order \(5\). Define the \(\mathbb F_2\)-linear automorphism
\[
\sigma(a,t,b)=(\alpha a,t,\beta b).
\]
Then \(\sigma\) has order \(15\). Set \(W_1=\mathbb F_4\oplus\mathbb F_2^9\) and \(W_2=\mathbb F_{16}\); these are \(\sigma\)-invariant and \(V=W_1\oplus W_2\).

For \(W_1\), the codimension-one subspace \(U_1=\mathbb F_2\oplus\mathbb F_2^9\) is \(\sigma\)-covering because \(\alpha\) acts transitively on \(\mathbb F_4^\times\). Conversely, every \(\sigma\)-covering subspace must contain the nine-dimensional fixed summand \(\mathbb F_2^9\): each fixed vector appearing in any \(\sigma\)-translate already belongs to the original subspace. Its image in the \(\mathbb F_4\) quotient must also be nonzero. Therefore
\[
h_\sigma(W_1)=1.
\]

For \(W_2\), regard \(\mathbb F_4\) as the unique subfield of \(\mathbb F_{16}\) with four elements. Since \(|\langle\beta\rangle|=5\) and \(|\mathbb F_4^\times|=3\),
\[
\mathbb F_{16}^\times=\langle\beta\rangle\mathbb F_4^\times.
\]
Consequently \(\bigcup_{j=0}^4\beta^j\mathbb F_4=\mathbb F_{16}\), so \(h_\sigma(W_2)\ge2\). A one-dimensional subspace has only one nonzero vector, and its five translates contain at most five nonzero vectors, whereas \(\mathbb F_{16}\) has fifteen. Hence
\[
h_\sigma(W_2)=2.
\]

Now \(U=U_1\oplus\mathbb F_4\) has codimension \(3\) in \(V\). For every \((a,t,b)\in V\), choose residues \(j_3\bmod3\) and \(j_5\bmod5\) such that \(\alpha^{-j_3}a\in\mathbb F_2\) and \(\beta^{-j_5}b\in\mathbb F_4\). The Chinese remainder theorem supplies \(j\bmod15\) satisfying both conditions. Thus \(\sigma^{-j}(a,t,b)\in U\), proving that \(U\) is \(\sigma\)-covering. Conversely, a codimension-four subspace has at most \(2^{11}\) elements, so its fifteen translates contain at most \(15\cdot2^{11}<2^{15}\) elements. Therefore
\[
h_\sigma(V)=3.
\]
Finally, the known identity \(h_q(q^d-1)=d-1\) gives \(h_2(15)=3\). Hence
\[
h_2(15)=h_\sigma(V)=3>
2=\max\{h_\sigma(W_1),h_\sigma(W_2)\},
\]
contradicting the proposed formula.
